newsitem.title: FRANCE: Erap chief hopes for New Caledonia mine deal soon.
newsitem.headline: Erap chief hopes for New Caledonia mine deal soon.

text.p: The head of state holding company Erap said on Monday that he hoped to get agreement soon on a controversial plan to build a new nickel smelter in New Caledonia.

Remy Chardon, who on Friday met the presidents of French nickel producer Eramet, Societe Miniere de Sud Pacifique (SMSP) and Canadian group Falconbridge, told Reuters in a telephone interview the talks were "very positive".
"The target is to get a draft agreement within a few weeks," Chardon said.
Erap owns 55 percent of Eramet, the world's third largest nickel producer.
In a joint statement released on Friday SMSP, Eramet and Falconbridge said they had found common ground for the smelter project.

"A broad exchange of views enabled us to realise that the three establishments shared a common concern of carrying out as quickly as possible a study by SMSP and Falconbridge of this investment," the statement said.

The statement also said experts would be brought in to study the problems identified during the meeting, the goal being to enable the "immediate" swap of assets between Eramet's Societe le Nickel (SLN) and SMPS.

The exchange involves SLN's Koniambo field and SMSP's Poum field. The nickel ore extracted from Koniambo would be used to supply a plant SMSP and Falconbridge plan to build in the north of the South Pacific island.
Eramet has repeatedly said it does not oppose the new smelter as long as it does not limit its development strategy in New Caledonia. But previous talks over a similar asset swap failed in February.
The state supports the new smelter project as part of a deal to appease local Kanak separatists ahead of a 1998 referendum on independence for the French territory.
Chardon said Friday's meeting had allowed all parties to make "significant progress" and to understand the demands and constraints of the others.
He said Falconbridge and SMSP had wanted to secure access to mining resources before starting feasibility studies for the smelter.
Eramet meanwhile wanted guarantees that the exchange of the mining titles would be fair and the nickel it supplied would be used exclusively to feed the smelter and not for exports.
Eramet also wanted guarantees that the exchange could be cancelled if the smelter was not built.

"The first result is that the partners accepted these constraints and the second is that Eramet agreed to discuss the terms and guarantees that would enable the immediate transfer of the mining titles. This is crucial. There is now a possible compromise on this issue." Chardon said.

Experts will meet "in coming days" to estimate the financial compensation that must be paid to Eramet as a result of the mining exchange. They will also establish a timetable for conducting the feasibility studies and work on the legal guarantees for the mining titles swap, he said.

Chardon became a board member of Eramet on April 16. In a newspaper interview last week he criticised the way Eramet's managers had handled the crisis in New Caledonia, saying they had wasted precious time.

Erap has also said that it wants to appoint a majority of directors on Eramet's board. If shareholders approve that motion at their annual meeting on May 29, it could pave the way for the ouster of chairman Yves Rambaud, industry sources have said.
"The state wants better control over the future of the company, notably its handling of New Caledonia, while strictly respecting the interests of the company," said Chardon.

"The state, Erap, wants a place on the board in line with its stake in Eramet. This move is not aimed at changing the industrial strategy of the company. That strategy will be continued. The state as the majority shareholder supports the interests of Eramet," he said.
